questions.q: Constant-rate SGD on $f(w) = \tfrac12\lambda w^2$ with gradient noise σ settles at an excess loss of $\eta\sigma^2 / (2(2-\eta\lambda))$. With $\eta\lambda$ small, what does halving η do to this floor?
options: Nothing — the floor depends only on σ
Doubles it, because steps get noisier
questions.explain: For small $\eta\lambda$ the floor is about $\eta\sigma^2/4$, proportional to η. That is why decaying schedules end below the constant one in Lab 2.

questions.q: In the warmup demo, $f(w) = \tfrac12 w^2 + \tfrac14 w^4$ and a step multiplies $w$ by $1-\eta(1+w^2)$. Starting at $w_0 = 3$, which constant rates avoid blowing up?
options: Any η, because the quartic has a single minimum
questions.explain: $|w|$ grows whenever $\eta(1+w^2) > 2$; at $w_0 = 3$ that means $\eta < 2/10 = 0.2$. Near the minimum $\eta < 2$ would be fine, which is why warming up to a larger η works.

questions.q: The inverse-square-root schedule is $\eta_{\max}\min\big(s/W,\ \sqrt{W/s}\big)$ with $s = t+1$. What is η at $s = 4W$?
questions.explain: After warmup $\eta = \eta_{\max}\sqrt{W/s} = \eta_{\max}\sqrt{1/4} = \eta_{\max}/2$: quadrupling the step count halves the rate.

questions.q: Why do LLM pretraining runs typically combine linear warmup with cosine decay?
options: Warmup avoids unstable large steps while the loss is sharp and Adam's statistics are unreliable; the decay lowers the SGD noise floor at the end
Warmup increases the batch size; cosine decay reduces the model size
Cosine decay is the only schedule that converges
Warmup is needed only because the data is shuffled
questions.explain: The start of training has high curvature (η < 2/λ allows only small steps) and immature optimizer statistics; later, shrinking η reduces the noise-driven loss floor. Warmup + cosine does both.
